prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: نتائج الانتخابات حسب الدائرة (language ar, right-to-left: column 1 is on the RIGHT).
Grid: 5 columns × 8 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Merged cells: "الدائرة" spans 1 col × 2 row; "المرشح أ" spans 2 col × 1 row; "المرشح ب" spans 2 col × 1 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 17px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "الدائرة" · longest unbreakable word 49px · one-line width 130px
  col 2: header "المرشح أ › الأصوات" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 58px
  col 3: header "المرشح أ › النسبة" · longest unbreakable word 50px · one-line width 50px
  col 4: header "المرشح ب › الأصوات" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 58px
  col 5: header "المرشح ب › النسبة" · longest unbreakable word 50px · one-line width 50px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 413px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 412px.
Fixed: content, font, 17px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"good","why":"All numbers and both header rows stay on one line and remain comparable, but the district column is squeezed so far that names stack into three lines (دائرة / المفرق / الأولى), making rows tall and the vertical rhythm heavy; still perfectly legible."},"B":{"grade":"good","why":"Same trade-off as A: figures intact and aligned, headers on one line, but district cells break into three short lines, inflating row height without adding information."},"C":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Best balance: numeric columns and headers each hold one line while the district column keeps two-line wraps (دائرة المفرق / الأولى), so rows read as compact units, numbers align in columns and the header block sits as a clean two-tier band."},"D":{"grade":"bad","why":"Widths collapse the data columns: numbers split mid-digits ('18,4 / 20', '13,9 / 05') and percentages split from their % sign, and the header 'النسبة' breaks into 'النسب / ة'. Values become unreadable and uncomparable."},"E":{"grade":"good","why":"Numbers and headers stay whole, but the district column is narrower than needed, forcing three-line cells in the upper rows while lower rows use two, giving an uneven row rhythm; acceptable but less tidy than C."},"F":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Equivalent to C in effect: figures on one line, headers intact, district names wrap at word boundaries in at most two lines, so rows stay compact and the two-candidate grouping under 'المرشح أ' / 'المرشح ب' reads clearly."}},"best":["C","F"],"confidence":"medium","unsure":"C and F look nearly identical at this rendering; the few pixels of difference in the district column are hard to judge, and I cannot tell whether A/B/E's extra row height would be considered acceptable in the intended publication context."}
